"The Singularity Is Near" by Ray Kurzweil
I didn't like this book.. bigoted techno-worshipping at it's finest, by the guru himself.

Um... okay? I don't recall any bigotry in the book, or any techno-worship (What does that even mean? Google searches just bring up a bunch of christian techno groups...). It is one thing to disagree with specific content of the book, it is another to just outright dismiss it with unsubstantiated labels and flippant sarcasm. I mean, I know Kurzweil is pretty smart, but I don't think he was very arrogant in the book (or claim to be a "guru"). He at least took the time to respond to his critics in some impressively calculated rebuttals.

By "techo-worship" I meant worship for Progress and Technology, the idea that the progress of humankind is necessarily linked to an increase of technological inventions, faster computers, smaller chips, AI, etc.

Sorry for the sarcasm, I was expressing my subjective opinion, maybe the wording was to harsh. This is no place to discuss individual points of Kurtzweils theory, I'll just post one link to the Wikipedia page listing some critiques of the Singularity.

I called him a guru because he's the author many people who believe technology is all that matters turn to. I used to be one of them and in the years following my reading of the book I steadily became more critical. When you consider how we are already destroying our ecosystem by mining for resources needed by our techno-structure, where will we find all the rare metals needed for all theses AIs and machines Kurzweil is predicting? In the end the whole idea seems very disconnected from the ecology of the planet. But maybe he has a solution for that, I confess I am not very up to date with his later thinking.

Endurance: Shackleton's Incredible Voyage

A great tale of adventure, and heroism in the exploration of Antarctica.

"Insanely Great" by Steven Levy is a now very dated enthusiastic history of Apple and what made you genuinely special at the dawn of personal computing. "Cyberia" by Douglas Rushkoff is about the entrance to the digital age as... Kind of transhumanism for the soul, from the perspective of a journalist hanging out with and doing drugs with the hackers and visionaries of the time. It's awesome.
Confessions of an Economic Hitman might be up your alley, but I think you should read that with your skepticism filter on.

The Four Agreements by Don Miguel Ruiz!

The Work of Nations by Robert Reich

A Brief History of Time by Stephen Hawking

Be Here Now by Ram Dass

The Tao of Physics by Fritjof Capra

The Exegesis of Phillip K. Dick by Philip K. Dick

Just to name a few :)

The Tao of Physics blew my mind when I was a teenager. An important read for both agnostic science oriented people as well as the more spiritual driven folks, it builds a convincing bridge between quantum physics and eastern mysticism.
Changed the way I thought about the world when I was 15

Recently finished "Mania," a book about the Beat generation. It fits the bill on historical politics, at least. Tries to be a bit gonzo, which doesn't always work perfectly, or even well, but it made for a decent story and I learned me a thing or two.

Amusing Ourselves to Death by Neil Postman.

It's focuses on how mass media has kept people passive and content and less worried about our political and economic situation. It's way more relevant now than when it was first published thirty years ago.
The Image: A Guide To Pseudo-Events in America by Daniel Boorstin is (sorta) similar and both would be a great in preparation for the election cycle.

The Boys in the Boat, Daniel James Brown

At Home: A short history of private life by Bill Bryson

The Social Conquest of Earth by E.O. Wilson

The Blind Watchmaker by Richard Dawkins

Kitchen Confidential by Anthony Bourdain

All The Shah's Men by Stephen Kinzer -- if you're looking for U.S. history this is the one you want to go for.

Under the Banner of Heaven by Jon Krakauer (also Into Thin Air

I know there are more that I really enjoyed but that's what I came up with for now

An excellent book I came across and have re-read is "All the Shah's Men" by Stephen Kinzer. It makes you understand why Iran hates the Western world, as we overthrew their democratically elected leader because the UK wanted to continue exploiting Iran for their oil. It explores the overthrowing of Mossadegh.
Currently reading The Autobiography of Malcolm X. It's an insightful read into the life of black rights activist and gives a look into the lives of Negros prior to the Civil Rights act.
Just wanted to say thank you all for the suggestions!

Not about US politics, but Green Was the Earth on the Seventh Day by Thor Heyerdahl is super interesting - fella and his wife kind of drop off the face of the earth to live on a remote island called Fatu Hiva, Survivor-style. Probably my favourite nonfiction!

J. Edgar Hoover: The Man and His Secrets by Curt Gentry

Ford: The Men and the Machine by Robert Lacy

The first is a very comprehensive history of the FBI under Hoover (who effectively created the organization and ran it for nearly 50 years) the second is a history of the American automotive industry. I loved reading both.

I am re-reading CULLODEN: The History and Archaeology of the Last Clan Battle I found/find it to be an exemplary book which uses detailed study, and a unique way to examine archaeology in a battlefield manner. You honestly feel like you understand the battle, for the first time. I am passionate about ancient warfare and this battle has been stymied by history. This was able to open my mind to the possibility that the battle NEARLY went the other way. Fascinating. Imagine the world today if it had?

It contains information concerning Culloden and the Clearances never discussed in other volumes. It is a great read if you are interested in Scotland, ancient battles, battlefield archeology.
US history, I would recommend "A People's History of the United States" by Howard Zinn.
I suggest The Long Descent by John Michael Greer, an "accurate diagnosis of the terminal illness our fossil-energy subsidized civilization has too long denied."

Not a book, but this 6-part essay is really in depth and interesting though it has a multitude of books to choose from in the bibliography for further reading.

Also everyone needs at least one Hitler book, so I say go with John Toland's biography. Has some nifty bits I don't see come up often elsewhere, like jewish veteran associations supporting the NSDAP due to fervent patriotism and a fear of communism. Seen in summaries of it around the net he interviewed over 200 people that lived through both wars and worked and ate alongside the big H before he ever became important until the very end. My version is a really old one I found at a garage sale and doesn't have a foreword though, just a "thanks and dedication" page at the start. Mild warning that it's just a little bit thicker than a bible, and probably more lethal.

Don't do a lot with US history past the cowboys and the revolution m'self. I just love the embellishments and spins every 'outlaw tale' gets in each revision, and how their currently-living families still argue with each other over versions of events.

If you want some weapon history to go along with your history history, The Great Warbow by Matthew Strickland's a pretty nice read.

Decision Points by George W Bush was an interesting read, He talks some about his earlier life and a lot about US Politics during his time in office. Sounds like something you might be interested in even if you aren't a fan of his politics.

Another good nonfiction read is Too Big to Fail. This one dives into the banking system and the banking crisis of 2008. Probably my favorite read in the last year.

Hope this helps!
"Beyonders: a World Without Heroes" by Brandon Mull and the next two books (Seeds of Rebellion and Chasing the Prophecy) are awesome!
Guns, Germs, and Steel is always a good choice. It covers how our current civilizations came to be and why others never really got here.
Rubicon: The Last Years of the Roman Republic by Tom Holland. Roman politicians were playing for keeps, and the intrigues that went on would make Frank Underwood blush!

For US history and things that influenced where we are now (and are interesting reads):

Command and Control by Eric Schlosser (almost a catastrophic oops...)

The Making of the Atomic Bomb by Richard Rhodes (self-explanatory)

A Bright Shining Lie by John Paul Vann (Vietnam)

A People's History of the United States by Howard Zinn (US history)

For interesting, semi-related nonfiction:

Dispatches by Michael Herr (if you've seen Full Metal Jacket or Apocalypse Now, this was hugely influential and sometimes directly pulled from)

The Forever War by Dexter Filkins (similar to the Herr book)

Fear and Loathing on the Campaign Trail '72 by Hunter S. Thompson (political journalism)

For great non-fiction:

Wind, Sand and Stars by Antoine Saint-Exupery (just a beautiful book)

In the Garden of Beasts by Erik Larson (Berlin while the Nazis grew in power)

In the Kingdom of Ice by Hampton Sides (an Arctic misadventure)

Lost in Shangri-la by Mitchell Zuckoff (a WWII plane crash on an island)

The Dust Bowl by Timothy Egan (this might be unfortunately relevant)

Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr. by Ron Chernow - very long book about Rockefeller but riveting and provides a fantastic overview of how the oil industry.

Guns, Germs and Steel: The Fates of Human Societies by Jared Diamond - this book gets a lot of flack for being biased but I found it a compelling argument and enjoyable read.

My husband also highly recommends the author Jon Ronson but I haven't gotten around to him yet - he has several books and essays published.

The Populist Moment: A Short History of the Agrarian Revolt in America by Lawrence Goodwyn is a seriously great book about politics, power, revolution, and economics which is highly relevant today. It's a condensed version of Democratic Promise, which is about twice as long but worth it.

Killing Lincoln. Some people may have problems with the author's political views, but this is all about Lincoln, no politics involved. I believe he was a history teacher before he became a pundit (O'Reilly, not Lincoln).
